messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Standard Error of the Mean (SEM)**  
For a one‑sample test the “standard deviation” you need is actually the **standard error of the mean**, which quantifies how much the sample mean would vary if you repeatedly drew samples of the same size from the population.

\[
\text{SEM}= \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

where  

* \(s = 1.4\) (the sample’s observed standard deviation)  
* \(n = 40\) (the sample size)

---

### Calculation

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{n}&=\sqrt{40}\approx 6.32456\\[4pt]
\text{SEM}&=\frac{1.4}{6.32456}\\[4pt]
&\approx 0.2217
\end{aligned}
\]

Rounded to three decimal places:

\[
\boxed{\text{SEM}\;\approx\;0.222}
\]

This value represents the expected spread of the sample means around the *true* population mean (\(\mu_0 = 98.6\)) under the null hypothesis. It will serve as the denominator when computing your test statistic (e.g., a t‑statistic):

\[
t = \frac{\bar{x}-\mu_{0}}{\text{SEM}}\; .
\]
